new_statements.quote: [p. 69] Fakamae has a stress system of right-aligned moraic trochees. It is a head foot left system, meaning that in words which contain more than one foot, it is the left foot which carries the primary stress. [...] This regular stress pattern is overridden by a ‘weight-to-stress’ system (Prince, 1990), whereby a single syllable foot draws primary stress to itself, regardless of its position within a word. [p. 70] In Fakamae, heavy syllables are those which contain long vowels or diphthongs. Codas do not carry morae in Fakamae [...]. [...] They are right-aligned, meaning that they align with the right edge of the word. Regular stress in Fakamae is therefore penultimate.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Mae as fixed antepenultimate, quantity-insensitive (gordon: antepenultimate stress, from Capell 1962:6 via Gordon 2002). Dewar 2022 (the deposit's thesis bundle, read from the Newcastle copy we hold) analyses Fakamae stress as quantity-SENSITIVE right-aligned moraic trochees with REGULAR PENULTIMATE stress: trisyllabic all-light words are stressed on the penult ([t̪ø.ˈrɐ.ŋɐ] 'time', [ɐ.ˈvɐ.ŋɐ] 'marry'), where the catalog's 100 predicts the initial; four-light-syllable words take primary stress on the initial with secondary on the penult ([ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ]), where the catalog's 0100 predicts the second syllable; words ending in a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on the f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, right-aligned moraic trochees. Heavy syllables = long vowel or diphthong (two morae); codas are weightless. Regular stress falls on the penultimate MORA: penultimate syllable in all-light words ([t̪ø.ˈrɐ.ŋɐ] 'time', [ki.ˈmœ.ɐ] 'rodent', [ˈke.re] 'ground'), final syllable when the word ends in a heavy syllable ([ɐ.ˈfɐː] 'hurricane', [t̪œ.ˈkɐi] 'rafter'). Suffixes shift stress rightward ([ˈt̪ø.si] 'book' -> [t̪ø.ˈsi.jɐ] 'write-TR'). In words of two or more feet the LEFT foot carries primary stress (head-foot-left): four light syllables -> primary on the initial, secondary on the penult ([ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ] 'back', [ˈfɐ.t̪i.ˌt̪i.ri] 'lightning'); but a monosyllabic (heavy) foot attracts primary stress wherever it stands (weight-to-stress: [ˌbɐ.kɐ.ˈkɐø] 'wing', [ˌtø.wɐ.ˈŋɐː.n̪e] 'woman's brother', [ˌfɐ.kɐ.ˈt̪ɐø.ˌvi.jɐ] 'buy'); if several heavy feet occur the leftmost takes primary stress ([ˈrɐː.ˌkɐø] 'tree').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: every non-head foot carries secondary stress on its strong (first) mora, e.g. [ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ] 'back', [ˈmɐː.ˌsi.n̪ɐ] 'moon', [fɐ.ˈkɐː.ˌrœ.fɐ] 'be poor', [ˌt̪ɐf.t̪ɐ.ˈfɐː.ki] 'sides' (Tables 2.24-2.26, pp. 72-74).
new_statements.exceptions: Weight-to-stress overrides the head-foot-left default (2.7.2); CVC reduplicant prefixes never attract stress because codas are non-moraic ([pœt̪.ˈpœ.t̪ø] 'ends', [sɐt̪.ˈsɐː.t̪i] 'be bad', 2.7.3); the nominaliser -ɐŋɐ elides after root-final /ɐ/ giving variable [mø.ˈn̪ɐː.ŋɐ] ~ [mø.ˈn̪ɐ.ŋɐ] (2.7.1); vowel syncope between stressed syllables is treated in 2.5.1.2 (p. 61). No lexical exceptions are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Fakamae (Emae, Mae; mmw), the Polynesian Outlier of Makatea and Tongamea villages on south-western Emae island, Shefa Province, Vanuatu (c. 200 speakers on Emae); Dewar's 2018-2019 recordings were made mainly in Tongamea with consultants such as Willie Kalo Jacob, Jerry Malesu Jacob and Leising Leiseroto Manuriki; the same language Capell 1962 described as 'Mae (Emwae)'. The thesis notes heavy multilingualism (Bislama, Namakura) in the community.

readall_conflicts: Dewar 2022, the one openly accessible component of this ELAR deposit (its PhD-thesis bundle, read from the Newcastle copy we hold), contradicts the catalog record for Mae (fixed antepenultimate, quantity-insensitive: gordon antepenultimate stress, sourced to Capell 1962:6 via Gordon 2002): Dewar analyses Fakamae stress as right-aligned moraic trochees, regular stress PENULTIMATE, heavy syllables (long vowels, diphthongs; codas weightless) attracting primary stress anywhere in the word, and head-foot-left primary stress otherwise, so that trisyllabic light words are penult-stressed [t̪ø.ˈrɐ.ŋɐ] (catalog: initial), four-light-syllable words are initial-stressed with penult secondary [ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ] (catalog: second syllable), and words ending in a heavy syllable are final-stressed [ɐ.ˈfɐː]. The catalog's Capell quote as recorded is itself internally inconsistent ('normally antepenultimate' followed by 'a small number of examples of antepenultimate accentuation can be adduced, e.g. 'nanafi, 'taŋata'), which suggests the first word may be 'penultimate' in Capell's text; if so Dewar agrees with Capell's default and only the Gordon/StressTyp antepenultimate coding is contradicted. The Capell 1962 p. 6 scan held by the project should be re-checked on that word before the record is revised. The deposit's own metadata is silent on stress.

audit.recode_to: Not fixed antepenult. reclassify from Dewar 2022 §2.7 (pp. 69-74): quantity-sensitive, right-to-left (right-aligned) moraic trochees with End Rule LEFT (primary stress in the leftmost foot) and weight-to-stress override (CVV/CVː syllables take primary stress wherever they sit; codas weightless). All-light words: 2σ 10, 3σ 010 (penult), 4σ 1000, 5σ 01000, 6σ 100000, i.e. stress on syllable 2 of 3, 1 of 4, 2 of 5, 1 of 6, 2 of 7, 1 of 8 for the light-syllable default, not in the strict set (weight-sensitive), secondary stress on remaining foot heads; suffixes shift stress rightward (t̪ø.ˈsi.jɐ 'write-TR'). Cite Dewar 2022:69-72, Tables 2.21-2.25; demote Capell 1962:6 / StressTyp2 209 / Gordon 2002 to 'superseded; Capell's sentence misprinted (his own tu'raŋa is penult)'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the Capell 1962:6 passage carried in the record is verbatim on the page image we hold ( cap_tiff/, opened visually) — but the record's formal quote/cite/grade fields are empty and the class rests on Gordon 2002's appendix via StressTyp2; Capell's sentence is self-contradictory and his examples show penult. (2) Deciding source: a 2002 typological survey reading a 1962 55-pp sketch; the best source is Dewar 2022, a 624-pp fieldwork PhD grammar with a six-page stress analysis, which we already hold but never used for stress. (3) Dewar contradicts the classification on every count that matters: trisyllables are penult [t̪ø.ˈrɐ.ŋɐ], quadrisyllables initial [ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ], odd-parity words second-syllable, and heavy syllables attract primary stress anywhere in the word (weight-to-stress). So Mae is neither 'single/fixed' nor 'antepenult'; it is a parity-dependent
